track.subject: Mathematics
track.description: A connected K–12 planning skeleton: number and shape develop into algebra, geometry, functions, statistics, and optional advanced modeling.
track.scopeNote: Original unit plans aligned to the 2010 Common Core mathematics standards. K–8 placements follow grade-specific expectations; grades 9–12 use an authored Algebra 1 → Geometry → Algebra 2 → optional advanced-functions/modeling sequence, not an official grade assignment or graduation rule. Each course budgets 36 instructional weeks including practice, assessment, and reteaching; schedules are adaptable. The registry uses the PDF domain plus numbered-standard identifiers (for example 8.EE.7 and A-REI.4), without the optional web namespace/cluster-letter expansion. Each numbered entry includes all lettered subparts, with concise topic labels rather than the official full wording. Mapping a parent code identifies a planned encounter, not evidence that every subpart is mastered in that unit; repeated high-school codes progressively cover function families and methods. Entire (+) numbered standards are marked extension. F-IF.7d, F-BF.1c, and F-BF.4b–d are optional (+) subparts of otherwise core parent entries and are planned in the optional Grade 12 pathway. Mathematical practices recur across grades and units; their unit references are intentional emphases, not exclusive placements. High-school Modeling has no standalone numbered standards: modeling is woven through quantity, algebra, function, geometry, and statistics work. These are full-year scope-and-sequence outlines, not completed daily lessons, exercises, textbook reproductions, official certification, or evidence of learner mastery.

courses.title: Counting, shapes, and number stories
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Bring everyday experiences of grouping, sharing, and noticing shapes; no reading or formal arithmetic prerequisite.
outcomes: Count and compare collections accurately.
Represent addition/subtraction within 10 and become fluent within 5.
Describe shapes, measurements, and teen quantities.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 1: Ten ones become the bundled ten used for Grade 1 place value; spoken number stories become equations with unknowns.
courses.yearBridge: Start with one-to-one counting, compare collections, join and separate quantities, organize numbers around ten, then use measurement and shape building to explain a complete number story.
courses.crossSubject: Retell a read-aloud sequence with first/next/last; describe objects and explain a drawing orally before an adult records the words.
routines: Use counters, drawings, talk, and gestures before connecting to written symbols.
Revisit small-number combinations in brief games; explain a strategy without speed pressure.
Ask a partner to show the same quantity another way, then check by counting.

units.title: Counting collections
units.focus: Connect number words, objects, and written numerals.
learning: Match one count word to each object and explain why rearranging a set preserves its count.
Read and write numerals 0–20 while gradually extending the oral count to 100 by ones and tens.
activities: Make a counting tray for a partner, including an empty tray.
Place classroom objects above, below, and beside a box and describe the arrangement.
evidence: Count arranged sets through 20 and scattered sets through 10 without omissions.
Show the collection named by a numeral and explain the last count word.
units.bridge: Reliable counts make comparison possible.

units.title: Comparing and making groups
units.focus: Use matching and counting to compare quantities and notice shape features.
learning: Compare groups through 10 and numerals 1–10.
Name flat and solid shapes even when turned or resized.
activities: Match pretend cups to plates and decide which collection has more.
Sort rotated shape cards and solids; explain why color does not determine shape.
evidence: Defend a more/less/equal claim with a matching or counting demonstration.
Name a rotated triangle and distinguish a flat circle from a sphere.
units.bridge: Comparing groups leads to adding or removing objects to change them.

units.title: Joining and separating
units.focus: Act out addition and subtraction before recording the mathematics.
learning: Represent joining and separating within 10 with objects, drawings, and spoken explanations.
Find more than one two-part decomposition and build fluency within 5.
activities: Tell a story about toy animals arriving and leaving; let a partner model it.
Hide part of a small collection and explain how many are hidden.
evidence: Match a drawing to an addition or subtraction story.
Find two decompositions of the same total and check by recombining.
units.bridge: Number parts support making ten.

units.title: Ten and some more
units.focus: Use ten as a visible organizing structure.
learning: Find the missing part that makes 10 from quantities 1–9.
Represent 11–19 as ten individual ones and additional ones.
activities: Fill a ten-frame and describe its empty spaces.
Build teen-number trays with a full ten-frame and loose counters; draw each part.
evidence: Show the complement to ten and explain the count.
Compose a teen quantity and identify the ten ones without treating the digits as separate totals.
units.bridge: Stable number structures make measurement records easier to organize.

units.title: Measuring and sorting
units.focus: Compare visible attributes and organize small collections.
learning: Describe more than one measurable property of an object.
Compare shared attributes directly and classify/count categories of at most 10.
activities: Compare ribbons by lining up endpoints, then compare classroom objects by weight using a balance.
Sort a collection by one chosen feature, record category counts, and solve a joining story from the groups.
evidence: Explain why a longer-looking ribbon may need aligned endpoints to compare fairly.
Count each category and show which has more without recounting an object.
units.bridge: Describing attributes also helps explain how shapes fit together.

units.title: Building and explaining
units.focus: Combine shape composition with a cumulative number-story workshop.
learning: Build and combine shapes, describing their parts and positions.
Use counting and ten-part reasoning to explain original addition/subtraction stories.
activities: Build a pretend park from shapes, then describe how two pieces form a larger figure.
Create a picture story with quantities through 10 and a separate teen collection for visitors.
evidence: Identify a shape by its properties after it is turned.
Independently model a new story, show a teen quantity, and demonstrate fluency within 5.
units.bridge: Carry composed numbers and precise descriptions into Grade 1.

courses.title: Tens, operations, and measurement
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Count collections through 20; compare small quantities.
Represent joining/separating within 10 and identify a ten with extra ones.
outcomes: Solve addition/subtraction problems within 20 with varied unknowns; be fluent within 10.
Use tens and ones to reason about numbers and calculations within 100.
Measure lengths, interpret small data displays, and partition shapes equally.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 2: Tens-and-ones strategies extend to hundreds; equal shares and rectangular arrangements prepare for fractions and arrays.
courses.yearBridge: Build tens and ones, develop within-20 operation strategies, express equality and place-value calculations, then apply them to length, time, data, and composed shapes before a classroom planning task.
courses.crossSubject: Read short problem sentences aloud, identify what changed and what is unknown, and write or dictate an explanation using because.
routines: Use counters, drawings, talk, and gestures before connecting to written symbols.
Revisit small-number combinations in brief games; explain a strategy without speed pressure.
Ask a partner to show the same quantity another way, then check by counting.

units.title: Numbers and equal groups of ten
units.focus: Rebuild cardinality and make the ten a reusable unit.
learning: Count/read/write through 120 from varied starting numbers.
Represent two-digit numbers with tens and ones and compare their values.
activities: Bundle craft sticks into tens and label several collections in different ways.
Start a number path at an unfamiliar two-digit number and explain each next number.
evidence: Match a numeral with tens/ones and justify a comparison.
Continue a sequence across a decade boundary without restarting at one.
units.bridge: Tens supply useful landmarks for calculation.

units.title: Addition and subtraction strategies
units.focus: Connect stories, missing addends, and flexible mental methods.
learning: Solve varied-unknown stories within 20 and three-addend stories totaling at most 20.
Use counting on, making ten, and operation properties; develop fluency within 10.
activities: Act out a story with a missing starting amount and compare two representations.
Arrange three small groups to make a ten before finding the total.
evidence: Explain subtraction using an addition relationship.
Solve within-20 tasks with an efficient understandable strategy, rather than only counting all.
units.bridge: Known relationships make equations meaningful.

units.title: Equality and place-value calculation
units.focus: Treat equality as balance and compute with tens and ones.
learning: Decide whether addition/subtraction equations are true and find missing numbers.
Add within 100, mentally change a quantity by ten, and subtract multiples of ten.
activities: Build both sides of an equation with counters, including the total on the left.
Show two ways to add a two-digit number and a one-digit number using bundles and drawings.
evidence: Explain why an equation remains true when an equivalent expression replaces one side.
Find ten more/less and explain which place changes.
units.bridge: Number differences can describe differences in length.

units.title: Length, time, and data
units.focus: Make comparable measurements and interpret simple records.
learning: Order lengths and measure with equal units without gaps or overlaps.
Read hours/half-hours and interpret up to three categories of data.
activities: Measure classroom paths using the same-size tiles and compare results.
Survey a classroom choice, build a three-category display, and connect a class schedule to clocks.
evidence: Demonstrate why changing unit size changes the count.
Read a half-hour clock and answer total/how-many-more questions about the display.
units.bridge: Equal measurement units prepare equal shares.

units.title: Shape parts and equal shares
units.focus: Describe defining properties and compose or partition figures.
learning: Separate defining shape attributes from color, size, and orientation.
Compose figures and partition circles/rectangles into halves and fourths.
activities: Make the same large shape with two different sets of pieces.
Fold paper rectangles into two or four equal shares and explain the size change.
evidence: Recognize a shape after rotation and justify the name with attributes.
Show equal shares and explain why more equal parts produce smaller shares.
units.bridge: Part-whole reasoning transfers back to number stories.

units.title: A classroom plan in numbers
units.focus: Coordinate counting, computation, measurements, and explanation.
learning: Choose operations for unfamiliar stories within 20 and defend the unknown.
Use place value, lengths, and categorical data to make a simple plan.
activities: Plan a pretend classroom supply shelf with tens bundles and a measured space.
Compare two proposed supply counts and write/dictate a correction when an equation misrepresents a story.
evidence: Solve a fresh unknown-start or comparison story without a named method.
Explain a within-100 sum and demonstrate fluent combinations within 10.
units.bridge: Grade 2 extends these units to hundreds and measurement tools.

courses.title: Hundreds, measurement, and arrays
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Use tens/ones and solve addition/subtraction stories within 20.
Measure with equal units and describe halves/fourths.
outcomes: Compute within 1000 with place-value reasoning and fluently within 100.
Solve one/two-step stories, measure standard lengths, and interpret time, money, and graphs.
Use arrays, equal shares, and attributes to prepare multiplication and fractions.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 3: Arrays and skip-counting become multiplication; equal-area partitions become numbered fractions in Grade 3.
courses.yearBridge: Extend place value to hundreds, justify regrouping, solve two-step everyday stories, measure and display lengths, and connect arrays and equal shares in a cumulative design.
courses.crossSubject: Read two-step directions in sequence; label graphs clearly and write a short explanation linking a measurement to a claim.
routines: Use counters, drawings, talk, and gestures before connecting to written symbols.
Revisit small-number combinations in brief games; explain a strategy without speed pressure.
Ask a partner to show the same quantity another way, then check by counting.

units.title: Hundreds as units
units.focus: Extend place-value structure through 1000.
learning: Read/write/compare numbers through 1000 using hundreds, tens, and ones.
Skip-count by 5, 10, and 100 and connect word, numeral, and expanded forms.
activities: Bundle a pretend collection into hundreds and trade a hundred for tens.
Build a number with specified digits, then change its value by ten or one hundred.
evidence: Explain a three-digit comparison using the first differing place.
Represent a number in all three forms and predict a mental change.
units.bridge: Place-value trades support larger calculations.

units.title: Strategies for adding and subtracting
units.focus: Explain regrouping before relying on written procedures.
learning: Add/subtract within 1000 with concrete or drawn place-value support.
Develop fluency within 100 and mental fluency within 20, including one-digit sums from memory.
activities: Compare a trade-based drawing with a compensation strategy for the same subtraction.
Combine up to four two-digit collections and explain convenient groupings.
evidence: Show why regrouping preserves a quantity.
Calculate independently, then explain or repair a place-value error.
units.bridge: Computation becomes a tool for multistep situations.

units.title: Stories, money, and clocks
units.focus: Represent unknowns and sequence two related operations.
learning: Solve one/two-step stories within 100 with unknowns in varied positions.
Use dollar/cent notation and read time to five minutes with a.m./p.m.
activities: Run a pretend supply stand using coins and dollar bills.
Draw a two-step story with a missing starting amount and annotate a five-minute clock schedule.
evidence: Identify the intermediate quantity before completing a story.
Make the same coin value two ways and read a clock with the correct time period.
units.bridge: Number lines provide a shared model for time and distance.

units.title: Measuring and displaying lengths
units.focus: Select tools and compare measurements with consistent units.
learning: Measure/estimate in inches, feet, centimeters, and meters; explain effects of unit size.
Solve length-difference stories and organize measurement data in line plots and graphs.
Represent whole numbers as distances from zero on an equally spaced number line and show sums and differences within 100 as directed moves.
activities: Measure one object using two units and compare the numerical results.
Measure a collection of paper strips, make a line plot, and create a four-category bar graph from a separate sort.
Draw two number-line routes to the same sum, then show a subtraction as the distance between marked quantities; connect both diagrams to measured ribbon lengths.
evidence: Place a ruler origin correctly and report a unit.
Use a plot or graph to answer a comparison question and show the matching subtraction.
Label an equally spaced number line, show the start and each move for a sum or difference within 100, and explain why the endpoint or distance answers the question.
units.bridge: Repeated equal units lead to rows and columns.

units.title: Arrays, parity, and shape attributes
units.focus: Organize equal groups and investigate parts of shapes.
learning: Explain odd/even collections through 20 by pairing.
Use arrays up to 5 by 5 and equal-square rectangle partitions; describe shape attributes and equal shares.
activities: Arrange counters into rectangles and record row sums in an equation.
Partition two equal rectangles into thirds with different-looking pieces and compare the equal shares.
evidence: Explain why a collection is even or has one unmatched object.
Draw a shape meeting stated attributes and count array squares without counting each individually.
units.bridge: Arrays become a model for multiplication and area.

units.title: Design, record, and justify
units.focus: Combine number operations with measurement and data.
learning: Choose a representation for a two-step situation and verify its result.
Use measurement, arrays, and data to explain a classroom design.
activities: Design a pretend display with small rectangular arrays and measured paper borders.
Write a short report comparing two layouts, using a graph and a two-step calculation.
evidence: Explain each quantity and unit in the final design.
Solve a fresh calculation within 1000 and show a mental strategy within 20.
units.bridge: Use the same arrays and part-whole explanations in Grade 3.

courses.title: Multiplication, fractions, and area
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Add/subtract within 1000 with place-value reasoning.
Interpret equal rows/columns and equal shares of shapes.
outcomes: Multiply/divide within 100 fluently and recall one-digit products.
Represent fractions as numbers and justify simple equivalences.
Connect area to multiplication and solve measurement/data problems.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 4: Multiplicative structures extend to larger numbers and comparison; fraction units support equivalent fractions and fraction operations.
courses.yearBridge: Develop equal-group meaning and operation properties, apply multiplication to area, locate fractions as numbers, interpret measured data, and combine these tools in two-step problems.
courses.crossSubject: Distinguish a problem question from background details; explain an arithmetic pattern with a labeled model and a short paragraph.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Equal groups and inverse operations
units.focus: Give multiplication and division meaning before fluent recall.
learning: Interpret products, sharing/grouping quotients, and missing factors.
Solve equal-group, array, and measurement stories within 100.
activities: Arrange equal collections with the same total and compare groups versus group size.
Write two division stories represented by the same array.
evidence: Distinguish number of groups from objects per group.
Solve a missing-factor equation and connect it to division.
units.bridge: Arrays reveal useful operation properties.

units.title: Properties, facts, and arithmetic patterns
units.focus: Use known products to derive others and explain computation.
learning: Apply multiplication properties and develop fluency within 100.
Explain arithmetic patterns, round to tens/hundreds, and add/subtract within 1000 fluently.
Multiply a one-digit whole number by a multiple of ten from 10 through 90 using place value and operation properties.
activities: Split an unfamiliar array into two known arrays and compare strategies.
Find a pattern in a multiplication table and justify it using groups, then estimate a related larger total.
Represent several groups of tens with bundles and an array; relate the total number of tens to the corresponding one-digit multiplication fact.
evidence: Recall one-digit products by year end and explain a useful derived fact.
Compute a multidigit sum/difference and use rounding as a check.
Solve a one-digit-by-multiple-of-ten product and explain why the result counts tens, rather than treating an appended zero as an unexplained rule.
units.bridge: Multiplication can count square units.

units.title: Area, perimeter, and shapes
units.focus: Distinguish covering a region from measuring its boundary.
learning: Measure rectangle/composite area using square units and multiplication.
Solve perimeter problems and classify quadrilaterals by shared properties.
activities: Build rectangles with equal perimeter but different area using tiles.
Decompose a stepped floor plan and explain why adding subareas works.
evidence: Label area in square units and perimeter in length units.
Find a missing side from a perimeter and identify the quadrilateral category.
units.bridge: Equal-area parts provide a model for fraction units.

units.title: Fractions as numbers
units.focus: Connect equal parts, number-line distances, and equivalence.
learning: Represent unit/nonunit fractions on a number line, using denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Explain simple equivalent fractions and compare same-numerator or same-denominator fractions referring to the same whole.
activities: Build fraction strips for one shared whole and place their lengths on a number line.
Challenge a comparison based on pictures of unequal wholes and repair the model.
evidence: Locate a fraction beyond one and name its unit fraction.
Justify equivalence or comparison with an accurate model and appropriate symbols.
units.bridge: Fraction units can describe measured lengths.

units.title: Time, mass, volume, and data
units.focus: Choose units and read information from scaled displays.
learning: Read time to a minute and solve elapsed-time situations.
Measure mass/liquid volume and interpret scaled graphs and half-/quarter-unit line plots.
activities: Plan durations for a pretend workshop on a timeline.
Measure strips to quarter units, display them, and compare with a scaled bar graph of supply categories.
evidence: Explain the difference between a graph symbol and the quantity it represents.
Solve a time or measurement problem with a matching equation and unit.
units.bridge: Measurement situations combine several operations.

units.title: Connected problem solving
units.focus: Use all four operations and defend a model.
learning: Solve two-step stories, identifying an intermediate quantity and estimating reasonableness.
Combine multiplication, area, and fraction representations in an original plan.
activities: Plan a tiled reading corner with grouped supplies, a boundary, and an equal-share display.
Exchange solutions and find a statement that confuses additive and multiplicative reasoning.
evidence: Solve an unfamiliar two-step task without an operation cue.
Explain a fraction location, an area calculation, and a multiplication/division relationship.
units.bridge: Grade 4 extends these structures to larger quantities and fraction operations.

courses.title: Whole-number structure and fraction operations
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Use multiplication/division facts and area models.
Represent fractions on number lines and explain simple equivalence.
outcomes: Compute with larger whole numbers and interpret remainders.
Compare and operate on fractions within Grade 4 limits; connect tenths/hundredths to decimals.
Use units, angle measurement, and shape properties in problems.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 5: Equivalent fractions prepare unlike-denominator operations; place-value scaling extends to thousandths and decimal computation.
courses.yearBridge: Use place value and multiplicative comparison to compute with larger numbers, develop equivalent fractions and fraction operations, connect decimals to measurement, then defend a multistep design.
courses.crossSubject: Annotate multistep problem constraints; distinguish a general rule from an example and write a justified comparison using precise terms.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Place value and multiplicative comparison
units.focus: Distinguish tenfold place changes from additive changes.
learning: Read/compare/round whole numbers through 1,000,000 and fluently add/subtract with standard algorithms.
Interpret how many times as many and distinguish it from how many more.
activities: Build a place-value chart and trace the effect of moving the same digit one place.
Draw paired tape diagrams for additive and multiplicative comparisons.
evidence: Explain the tenfold value change rather than merely naming a place.
Write and solve an equation matching a multiplicative-comparison story.
units.bridge: Multiplicative structure supports larger products and quotients.

units.title: Multiplication, division, and patterns
units.focus: Connect decomposition to written computation and contextual remainders.
learning: Multiply up to four digits by one digit and two digits by two digits; divide up to four digits by one digit.
Find all factor pairs for numbers 1–100, classify primes/composites, identify multiples, and solve multistep stories with sensible remainders.
Generate number or shape patterns from a stated rule and describe an additional feature that the rule does not explicitly name.
Distinguish prime and composite whole numbers through 100 from their factor pairs, including why 1 is neither.
activities: Compare an area model with partial products for the same multiplication.
Plan equal-size supply packs, interpret a remainder, and explain a factor-based packing choice.
Start a sequence at 2 and repeatedly add 5; investigate the alternating parity and repeating ones digits, then compare with a shape-growth pattern.
Arrange selected collections into every possible rectangular array, organize the factor pairs, and sort the totals into prime, composite, or neither.
evidence: Relate each partial product or quotient to place value.
Explain whether a remainder should be kept, discarded, or rounded up in a given context.
Continue a new rule-based pattern and justify one observed feature beyond simply restating the rule; explain why the feature should persist.
Give a complete factor-pair list and justify a prime/composite classification; correctly exclude 1 from both categories.
units.bridge: Factors and equal-size parts support equivalent fractions.

units.title: Equivalent fractions and comparisons
units.focus: Hold the whole fixed while changing the partition.
learning: Explain equivalent fractions by multiplying numerator/denominator by the same number.
Compare fractions using benchmarks or common units; use denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100.
activities: Refold fraction strips and record the same amount with different partitions.
Measure a small collection to eighths, plot the values, and defend an ordering.
evidence: Justify an equivalence with a model instead of only a rule.
Compare unlike fractions with a consistent whole and a stated reason.
units.bridge: Common fraction units make addition meaningful.

units.title: Fraction operations and decimals
units.focus: Operate on common fractional units and connect decimal notation.
learning: Add/subtract like-denominator fractions and mixed numbers; multiply a fraction by a whole number.
Connect tenths/hundredths, write decimal fractions, and compare decimals through hundredths.
Add a fraction in tenths to a fraction in hundredths by converting the tenths to equivalent hundredths; general unlike-denominator addition follows in Grade 5.
activities: Combine fractional lengths for a craft plan and explain repeated addition as a product.
Represent tenths and hundredths on the same grid and number line, including decimal notation.
Combine a tenths-grid amount with a hundredths-grid amount on the same-sized whole, record the regrouping in hundredths, and connect the sum to decimal notation.
evidence: Explain why denominators stay fixed in like-unit addition.
Solve a fractional-quantity story and justify a decimal comparison.
Show the equivalent hundredths before adding and explain why the units now match without treating this special case as a general unlike-denominator procedure.
units.bridge: Fractions and decimals now describe measured quantities.

units.title: Measurements, angles, and classification
units.focus: Use units and defining relationships to solve geometric problems.
learning: Convert to smaller units within one system and solve measurement/area/perimeter stories.
Measure/add angles; classify figures by line relationships and reflection symmetry.
activities: Design a rectangular sign with a specified perimeter and compare possible areas.
Construct an angle from adjacent parts, measure it, and test a proposed symmetry line by folding.
evidence: Distinguish linear, square, and angular units in a solution.
Identify parallel/perpendicular lines and justify a shape classification with attributes.
units.bridge: Measurement gives a setting for cumulative multistep reasoning.

units.title: Planning with whole and fractional quantities
units.focus: Integrate computation, models, and a written defense.
learning: Choose appropriate operations and units for a multistep plan.
Explain how an equivalent representation helps compute or check a result.
activities: Prepare a pretend exhibition plan with measured signs, grouped materials, and fractional lengths.
Compare two proposals and revise a calculation whose rounded answer violates a constraint.
evidence: Solve a new whole-number division problem and interpret its remainder.
Defend a fraction/decimal decision and explain each unit in the plan.
units.bridge: Grade 5 extends fraction units and decimal place value.

courses.title: Fraction arithmetic, decimals, and volume
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Compute multidigit whole numbers and explain fraction equivalence.
Add like-denominator fractions; interpret decimals through hundredths and rectangle area.
outcomes: Add/subtract unlike fractions and multiply fractions meaningfully.
Divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions; compute decimal quantities.
Connect volume, coordinate patterns, and classification hierarchies.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 6: Fraction division and decimal algorithms extend in Grade 6; paired patterns become variables, ratios, and relationships.
courses.yearBridge: Extend decimal place value, combine unlike fraction units, reason about fraction scaling and division, build volume from layers, and represent relationships with expressions and coordinate patterns.
courses.crossSubject: Translate verbal instructions into grouped expressions; write an explanation whose diagram, equation, units, and conclusion agree.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Place value and decimal operations
units.focus: Extend tenfold structure to decimals and powers of ten.
learning: Read/compare decimals to thousandths and round to a chosen place.
Multiply multidigit whole numbers fluently; divide with two-digit divisors and compute decimals through hundredths using models/strategies.
activities: Use a place-value chart to explain scaling by powers of ten without a moving-decimal shortcut.
Compare area/partial-quotient models for a whole-number and a related decimal calculation.
evidence: Explain a factor-of-ten relationship in both directions.
Check a decimal result with an estimate and show the quantity represented by each place.
units.bridge: Equivalent units also make fraction sums possible.

units.title: Adding and subtracting unlike fractions
units.focus: Create common units and judge the size of results.
learning: Add/subtract unlike-denominator fractions and mixed numbers.
Solve fraction-sum stories and use benchmarks to reject unreasonable answers.
activities: Combine measured fractional strips using a line plot as the data source.
Compare two common-denominator choices and show why both produce equal sums.
evidence: Show equivalent fractions before combining their numerators.
Explain why a result must fall between two benchmarks.
units.bridge: Fractions are quantities that can also be scaled and shared.

units.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
units.focus: Use area, sharing, and measurement models to explain operations.
learning: Interpret fractions as division and multiply fractions/mixed numbers.
Explain multiplication as scaling; divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
activities: Shade overlapping portions of a rectangle to derive a fractional product.
Compare sharing one unit fraction among several people with counting unit-fraction portions in several wholes.
evidence: Predict whether multiplication enlarges or shrinks a positive quantity before computing.
Distinguish the two allowed division forms and show a model; general fraction-by-fraction division belongs in Grade 6.
units.bridge: Fractional edge lengths will later extend volume reasoning.

units.title: Volume and measurement systems
units.focus: Build volume from layers of equal cubes.
learning: Explain cubic units and derive rectangular-prism volume from layers.
Add volumes of nonoverlapping prisms and convert standard units within a system.
activities: Build equal-volume boxes with different dimensions and compare layer counts.
Decompose a stepped solid into prisms and annotate a conversion used in its measurements.
evidence: Connect a cube count to both base-area-times-height and three-factor formulas.
Keep length, area, and volume units distinct and justify additivity.
units.bridge: Spatial organization prepares precise coordinate descriptions.

units.title: Expressions, coordinates, and hierarchies
units.focus: Represent calculations and relationships without losing their structure.
learning: Write/evaluate grouped expressions and compare two numerical patterns on a first-quadrant graph.
Classify figures using inherited properties and a hierarchy.
activities: Generate two related growing patterns, pair corresponding terms, and graph them.
Build a shape hierarchy, then test an always/sometimes/never claim about squares and rectangles.
evidence: Translate a spoken calculation into correctly grouped symbols.
Interpret a plotted point and explain why a shape inherits a broader category property.
units.bridge: Graphs and expressions become tools for modeling a complete situation.

units.title: A measured design and explanation
units.focus: Choose numerical and spatial models for a constrained plan.
learning: Coordinate fractions, decimals, units, and volume in multistep work.
Communicate a relationship with words, a table, a graph, and an expression.
activities: Plan a pretend storage system with box volumes and fractional material lengths.
Compare supply-cost patterns and explain the valid first-quadrant domain.
evidence: Solve fresh fraction and decimal tasks with independently justified models.
Present a design whose quantities, units, computations, and constraints agree.
units.bridge: Grade 6 uses these representations for ratios, variables, and signed quantities.

courses.title: Ratios, rational numbers, and expressions
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Operate with whole numbers/decimals and multiply fractions.
Interpret coordinates in the first quadrant, area/volume, and paired patterns.
outcomes: Use ratios, unit rates, and percentages to compare quantities.
Compute with fractions/decimals; locate and order signed rational numbers.
Model with expressions, equations, geometry, and distributions.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 7: Proportional relationships extend ratio reasoning; signed-number operations and multistep equations extend the number system.
courses.yearBridge: Consolidate fraction/decimal operations, compare quantities through ratios, extend coordinates across zero, introduce variable relationships, derive geometric measures, and describe statistical variability.
courses.crossSubject: Read tables and technical directions alongside prose; define quantities and units before writing an evidence-based explanation.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Arithmetic structure and fraction division
units.focus: Consolidate computation while explaining why operations work.
learning: Divide fractions by fractions and fluently use standard multidigit division/decimal algorithms.
Find greatest common factors of pairs at most 100 and least common multiples of pairs at most 12; use common factors to reorganize sums.
activities: Create both measurement and sharing interpretations of fraction quotients.
Compare a distributive factorization of a sum with its original computation.
evidence: Explain a fraction-division result with a model and multiplication check.
Calculate decimals with sensible scale and verify a common-factor/common-multiple claim.
units.bridge: Reliable arithmetic supports comparisons per one unit.

units.title: Ratios, rates, and percentages
units.focus: Move among ratio tables, diagrams, and contextual comparisons.
learning: Describe ratio relationships and unit rates; solve percentage and unit-conversion problems.
Use equivalent-ratio reasoning to justify comparisons rather than additive changes.
activities: Compare two invented mixtures with a double number line and ratio table.
Choose a better-value supply package after converting both prices to the same unit.
evidence: Explain the order and units in a ratio or rate.
Find a whole, part, or percentage from the other two and check against a benchmark.
units.bridge: Number lines extend in both directions to describe signed quantities.

units.title: Signed numbers and coordinates
units.focus: Separate magnitude, position, and contextual meaning.
learning: Locate rational numbers, opposites, and absolute values on number lines.
Use all four quadrants and find horizontal or vertical distances from coordinate positions and distances from zero: add magnitudes across zero and subtract the smaller magnitude on the same side.
activities: Build a signed elevation map and compare height with distance from sea level.
Reflect a coordinate polygon across an axis and determine horizontal/vertical side lengths using absolute values and positions relative to zero, without requiring general signed subtraction.
evidence: Explain why a negative number can have a large absolute value.
Plot and interpret ordered pairs in every quadrant; explain an axis-aligned distance using magnitudes and whether the points lie on the same or opposite sides of zero.
units.bridge: Coordinates and number relationships can be described with variables.

units.title: Expressions, equations, and dependencies
units.focus: Connect variables to quantities and solution sets.
learning: Evaluate exponent/variable expressions and justify equivalent forms.
Solve one-step equations, represent simple inequalities, and compare dependent/independent quantities in tables and graphs.
activities: Build two equivalent expressions for a tile border and verify them structurally.
Model a constant-rate situation in a table, graph, and equation; add a simple capacity constraint.
evidence: Distinguish an expression from an equation and a solution from an arbitrary input.
Substitute to check an equation solution and show all values satisfying a simple inequality.
units.bridge: Expressions organize area, surface area, and volume formulas.

units.title: Geometry through decomposition
units.focus: Derive measurements from familiar pieces.
learning: Calculate areas of triangles, quadrilaterals, and coordinate polygons.
Use nets for surface area and volume formulas for prisms with fractional edges.
activities: Cut and rearrange a triangle to explain its area formula.
Design a fractional-edge box, draw its net, and distinguish wrapping area from storage volume.
evidence: Justify a composite-area calculation without double-counting.
Give correct square/cubic units and relate the net to the solid.
units.bridge: Measurement produces variable data requiring a distribution view.

units.title: Questions, distributions, and evidence
units.focus: Describe variation rather than only one typical value.
learning: Distinguish statistical questions and describe distributions with shape, center, and variability.
Create dot plots/histograms/box plots and justify mean/median and variability summaries.
activities: Collect anonymous object-measurement data and display it in two ways.
Compare a dataset before and after a large outlier, including mean absolute deviation and interquartile range.
evidence: State sample size, units, center, spread, and an unusual feature in context.
Explain why a chosen summary fits the distribution and what the data cannot establish.
units.bridge: Grade 7 uses distributions to compare populations and study chance.

courses.title: Proportional reasoning, rational operations, and chance
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Use unit rates/percentages, rational coordinates, and one-step equations.
Interpret distributions, shape/center/spread, and area/volume models.
outcomes: Operate with signed rational numbers and solve multistep equations/inequalities.
Analyze proportional relationships and apply scale/percent reasoning.
Use geometry, random samples, and probability models to justify decisions.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 8: Linear functions extend proportional relationships; angle/scale reasoning becomes similarity and Pythagorean geometry.
courses.yearBridge: Extend signed arithmetic, recognize proportional relationships, express constraints algebraically, apply scale and geometry, then use sampling and probability to evaluate uncertain claims.
courses.crossSubject: Compare claims in quantitative reports, name the reference whole in percentage language, and explain uncertainty without overstating evidence.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Signed rational operations
units.focus: Extend operations coherently across zero.
learning: Add/subtract signed numbers with number-line reasoning and multiply/divide using operation properties.
Convert rational numbers to terminating/repeating decimals and solve four-operation stories.
activities: Model changes above and below a reference level and compare subtraction as adding an opposite.
Use distributivity to explain a negative-times-negative product, then check a rational computation.
evidence: Explain signs in context rather than reciting a sign rule.
Solve a mixed-form rational-number problem and justify its estimated magnitude.
units.bridge: Signed arithmetic supports proportional and algebraic models.

units.title: Proportional relationships and percent
units.focus: Recognize invariant ratios across representations.
learning: Calculate unit rates involving fractions and identify proportional tables/graphs/equations.
Solve multistep percent-change, interest, markup, discount, and percent-error problems.
activities: Compare proportional and fixed-fee pricing plans using tables and graphs.
Audit an invented sale advertisement with successive percentage changes and identify each reference whole.
evidence: Explain the significance of the origin and unit-rate point on a proportional graph.
Distinguish percent change from final percentage and check a reverse-percent result.
units.bridge: Equivalent expressions reveal the same proportional change.

units.title: Expressions, equations, and inequalities
units.focus: Use equivalent forms and preserve solution meaning.
learning: Expand/factor linear expressions with rational coefficients and explain their contextual meanings.
Solve multistep equations and inequalities, including rational coefficients, and interpret solution sets.
activities: Represent the same cost with a distributed expression and a factored one.
Write an equation and an inequality for two versions of a supply-limit problem; compare their graphs.
evidence: Check a candidate solution in the original relation.
Explain an inequality sign reversal when dividing by a negative number and retain contextual constraints.
units.bridge: Equations describe angle and scale relationships.

units.title: Scale and geometric measurement
units.focus: Connect proportionality with figures and solids.
learning: Use scale drawings, construct triangles from conditions, and describe plane slices of solids.
Solve circle, angle, composite-area, surface-area, and volume problems.
activities: Redraw a small floor plan at a new scale and compare length and area factors.
Build or sketch solids, predict cross-sections, and test whether triangle data permit one, many, or no triangles.
evidence: Explain why area scales differently from length.
Select circumference versus area appropriately and justify an angle equation or volume decomposition.
units.bridge: Measured quantities supply data for population comparisons.

units.title: Sampling and population comparisons
units.focus: Use random samples while acknowledging variation.
learning: Explain representative sampling and compare estimates across repeated random samples.
Compare distributions and draw limited population inferences using center and variability.
activities: Take repeated random samples from a visible collection with a hidden population summary.
Compare two measurement distributions and express the difference in centers relative to spread.
evidence: Identify a biased sampling method and propose a better one.
State a population comparison supported by the samples and describe uncertainty.
units.bridge: Repeated sampling shares structure with repeated chance trials.

units.title: Probability models and simulations
units.focus: Compare predicted chances with long-run evidence.
learning: Interpret probabilities from zero to one and build uniform/nonuniform models.
List compound-event sample spaces and simulate events to estimate probabilities.
activities: Design a two-stage chance device and enumerate its outcomes before testing it.
Compare observed frequencies with predictions and revise a model when unequal outcomes matter.
evidence: Distinguish equally named outcomes from equally likely outcomes.
Use a complete sample space or simulation to justify a probability and explain short-run variation.
units.bridge: Grade 8 connects variability and association to linear models.

courses.title: Real numbers, linear models, and geometric relationships
courses.scopeNote: Grade-specific Common Core content; 36 suggested instructional weeks include practice, assessment, and reteaching. Unit order is an authored planning choice.
prerequisites: Operate with signed rational numbers and solve equations/inequalities.
Understand proportional graphs, scale drawings, and probability/data displays.
outcomes: Use exponents, roots, and irrational approximations meaningfully.
Model linear relationships and solve systems; distinguish linear and nonlinear functions.
Explain transformations, similarity, Pythagorean relationships, volume, and bivariate association.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 9: The function concept and linear systems anchor Algebra 1; transformation arguments prepare formal Geometry proofs.
courses.yearBridge: Extend exact and approximate number representations, build linear equations and functions, solve simultaneous constraints, evaluate data models, and connect transformations to distance and volume.
courses.crossSubject: Compare a verbal claim with its graph and equation; explain assumptions and distinguish an observed association from a supported causal claim.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Real numbers and scale
units.focus: Extend number representations and control approximation.
learning: Convert repeating decimals to fractions and locate irrational values by rational bounds.
Apply integer exponent laws, square/cube roots, and scientific-notation arithmetic.
activities: Bracket an irrational length between successive rational approximations.
Compare invented very large and very small measurements in scientific notation, choosing sensible reporting precision.
evidence: Distinguish an exact root from its approximation and square-root equation solutions from the principal root.
Explain exponent transformations and compare orders of magnitude with units.
units.bridge: Accurate numeric reasoning supports equations and their checks.

units.title: Linear equations and rates
units.focus: Connect algebraic structure with proportional and linear graphs.
learning: Solve linear equations with one, no, or infinitely many solutions.
Interpret slope as unit rate; introduce informal similar triangles through familiar scale drawings to justify constant slope and y = mx + b, then revisit similarity formally in unit 5.
activities: Compare two forms of an equation to determine the number of solutions before finishing arithmetic.

Start with Grade 7 scale-drawing reasoning: enlarge a right triangle on a line and compare corresponding sides to informally justify equal rise/run. Revisit this argument after similarity transformations in unit 5.
evidence: Justify each equation step and test a solution by substitution.
Explain the difference between a proportional line and a line with nonzero intercept.
units.bridge: A rule connecting inputs and outputs can be studied as a function.

units.title: Functions and simultaneous constraints
units.focus: Compare relationships and find where two rules agree.
learning: Recognize functions, compare their representations, and construct linear models.
Solve two-variable linear systems graphically and algebraically and interpret zero/one/infinite solutions.
activities: Compare a verbal, tabular, and graphical pricing model, including a nonlinear counterexample.
Find when two delivery plans have the same cost and interpret both coordinates of the intersection.
evidence: Explain why a relation is or is not a function without relying only on a named test.
Check a system solution in both equations and explain what no intersection means.
units.bridge: Graph descriptions and equations support evidence-based data models.

units.title: Bivariate data and model limits
units.focus: Fit useful linear summaries without hiding uncertainty.
learning: Read scatter-plot associations and fit/interpret an informal linear model.
Use two-way tables and relative frequencies to compare categorical associations.
activities: Measure two nonpersonal properties of classroom objects and draw a reasonable line through the scatter.
Build a two-way table from an invented survey and compare conditional proportions, not just counts.
evidence: Interpret slope/intercept in context and flag an unreasonable extrapolation.
Support an association claim with appropriate relative frequencies while avoiding a causal conclusion.
units.bridge: Geometric transformations provide another way to compare related figures.

units.title: Transformations, congruence, and similarity
units.focus: Explain preserved and changed properties of figures.
learning: Describe rigid motions and dilations with coordinates.
Establish congruence/similarity through transformation sequences and argue angle sums, parallel-line angles, and AA similarity.
activities: Map a polygon to another using a sequence of moves and record coordinate changes.
Use a dilation and a parallel-line diagram to explain angle preservation and a triangle-angle relationship.
evidence: Identify which measurements survive each transformation.
Give a transformation sequence establishing congruence or similarity and explain why a failed example does not qualify.
units.bridge: Similarity and right triangles lead to distance formulas.

units.title: Pythagorean distance and solid volume
units.focus: Use geometric structure to solve spatial problems.
learning: Explain the Pythagorean theorem and its converse; calculate planar/spatial lengths and coordinate distances.
Calculate cylinder, cone, and sphere volumes and distinguish radius, diameter, and height.
activities: Rearrange square areas to explain a Pythagorean relationship, then test the converse.
Compare cylindrical and conical container capacities and find a diagonal route across a coordinate map.
evidence: Identify the right triangle and justify which length is the hypotenuse.
Give exact/approximate lengths as requested and report volume in cubic units.
units.bridge: Bring linear models to Algebra 1 and geometric explanations to formal proof.

courses.title: Algebra 1 — suggested high-school pathway
courses.scopeNote: Suggested high-school placement, not a Common Core grade mandate. The standards specify conceptual categories across grades 9–12. (+) content is optional advanced preparation; revisit core standards as indicated.
prerequisites: Solve Grade 8 linear equations/systems and interpret functions.
Use rational operations, integer exponents, and data plots.
outcomes: Build and solve linear, quadratic, and simple exponential models.
Connect equivalent expressions, equations, graphs, and sequences.
Describe data relationships and distinguish association from cause.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 10: Algebraic modeling supports coordinate Geometry; quadratics and exponential patterns are expanded systematically in Algebra 2.
courses.yearBridge: Define quantities and justify equations, connect linear functions and systems, contrast additive and exponential change, develop polynomial/quadratic structure, and evaluate algebraic models against data.
courses.crossSubject: Read a mathematical claim as an argument: define variables, quote the relevant given constraints, and explain why the conclusion follows.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Quantities, structure, and equations
units.focus: Make symbolic work accountable to units and meaning.
learning: Define quantities/units and appropriate precision; interpret expression parts and equivalent forms.
Create linear equations/inequalities and justify solution steps, including literal coefficients and rearranged formulas.
activities: Model a materials budget with clearly defined variables and unit conversions.
Compare two solution chains, finding the first step that fails to preserve equality.
evidence: Explain each term and its units and defend the reporting precision.
Solve a literal linear equation with needed restrictions and justify a rational/irrational combination.
units.bridge: Equations describe full sets of ordered pairs.

units.title: Linear functions and systems
units.focus: Coordinate algebraic and graphical solution sets.
learning: Use domains, ranges, notation, rates, and contextual graph features for linear and simple piecewise functions.
Model constraints with linear systems/inequalities and justify elimination.
Graph piecewise functions including step and absolute-value functions, with correctly included or excluded endpoints and meaningful domains.
activities: Compare a fixed-fee plan and a piecewise plan with a shared domain.
Draw feasible solutions to two resource constraints, then explain why an elimination step preserves the intersection.
Graph an invented delivery fee charged per started distance band and a separate distance-from-a-target rule; compare a step graph with an absolute-value graph.
evidence: Interpret a domain restriction and average rate with units.
Check a solution against every constraint and distinguish a point from a feasible region.
Evaluate at and beside a step boundary, mark its endpoint convention correctly, and connect both branches of an absolute-value graph to the defining rule.
units.bridge: Linear change provides a benchmark for exponential change.

units.title: Sequences and exponential growth
units.focus: Distinguish additive recurrence from multiplicative recurrence.
learning: Write explicit/recursive arithmetic and geometric sequences as functions on integer inputs.
Construct and compare linear/exponential models and interpret growth/decay factors.
activities: Create two growing-pattern stories with equal starting values but different change rules.
Compare an invented savings schedule using a fixed addition versus a constant percentage and state model assumptions.
evidence: Translate recurrence to an explicit formula and explain the discrete domain.
Use equal differences/factors to justify a model choice and interpret its parameters.
units.bridge: Products and repeated structure lead to polynomial expressions.

units.title: Polynomial structure and quadratic forms
units.focus: Use equivalent expressions to expose graph features.
learning: Add/subtract/multiply polynomials and factor accessible quadratics.
Connect standard, factored, and vertex forms to zeros, symmetry, and extrema.
activities: Represent a rectangular border area in two polynomial forms and reconcile them.
Transform a basic parabola and compare how factored and completed-square forms reveal different features.
evidence: Explain a factorization by expansion and identify meaningful zeros.
Sketch a quadratic with labeled vertex/intercepts and justify a transformation.
units.bridge: Quadratic structure suggests multiple solution methods.

units.title: Solving and interpreting quadratic models
units.focus: Choose methods by structure and check contextual solutions.
learning: Complete the square and derive/use the quadratic formula for real-root cases; revisit nonreal roots in Algebra 2.
Solve simple linear/quadratic systems and compare function intersections.
activities: Model a variable-dimension rectangle with a fixed area and evaluate which algebraic solutions fit.
Compare graphical, factoring, and completing-square approaches to the same quadratic.
evidence: Explain why a solution method applies and check the original equation.
Interpret each root or intersection and reject only those excluded by stated constraints.
units.bridge: Models fitted to data require a different kind of checking.

units.title: Data, association, and algebraic modeling
units.focus: Evaluate how well a model represents evidence.
learning: Compare univariate distributions with shape-appropriate center/spread measures.
Use two-way tables, regression, residuals, and correlation while distinguishing association from causation.
activities: Fit a line to original object-measurement data and inspect residual patterns.
Compare two written claims about an invented dataset and explain which overstates the evidence.
evidence: Interpret slope/intercept and correlation in context; identify a nonlinear residual pattern.
Present a model with a valid domain, unit labels, and an explicit limitation.
units.bridge: Carry equations and graph reasoning into Geometry; revisit distributions in Algebra 2 inference.

courses.title: Geometry — suggested high-school pathway
courses.scopeNote: Suggested high-school placement, not a Common Core grade mandate. The standards specify conceptual categories across grades 9–12. (+) content is optional advanced preparation; revisit core standards as indicated.
prerequisites: Use Algebra 1 equations, functions, and coordinate models.
Understand transformations, similarity, right triangles, and basic volume.
outcomes: Construct geometric proofs using definitions, transformations, and algebra.
Model with triangle trigonometry, circles, coordinates, and solids.
Use sample spaces and conditional probability to examine chance claims.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 11: Proof and coordinate structure support Algebra 2 function analysis; radians and right-triangle ratios lead to unit-circle trigonometry.
courses.yearBridge: Begin with transformations and precise constructions, establish congruence proofs, extend to similarity and trigonometry, connect circles and coordinates, model solids, and reason with conditional probabilities.
courses.crossSubject: Read a proof as a sequence of warranted claims; distinguish a definition, given fact, conjecture, and counterexample in an explanatory paragraph.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Transformations, definitions, and constructions
units.focus: Develop precise language and connect constructions to invariants.
learning: Define geometric objects and rigid motions and represent their effects.
Analyze polygon symmetries and make justified compass/straightedge or equivalent constructions.
activities: Construct an inscribed square or regular hexagon and explain the preserved distances.
Compare two sequences of rigid motions and predict their effects on a polygon.
evidence: Distinguish a construction from an approximate drawing and state its justification.
Describe a transformation precisely enough for another student to reproduce it.
units.bridge: Rigid motions provide the definition used in congruence proofs.

units.title: Congruence and proof
units.focus: Move from convincing examples to general arguments.
learning: Derive triangle congruence criteria through rigid motions.
Prove line/angle, triangle, and parallelogram theorems and use corresponding parts correctly.
activities: Build a proof of a triangle theorem using a carefully chosen auxiliary line.
Critique a diagram-based congruence claim and identify a missing hypothesis or counterexample.
evidence: State why a congruence criterion applies before using corresponding parts.
Write a proof with each conclusion supported by a definition, given, or established theorem.
units.bridge: Similarity keeps angle structure while allowing scale to change.

units.title: Similarity and right-triangle trigonometry
units.focus: Use invariant ratios to solve indirect-measurement problems.
learning: Establish dilation properties, AA similarity, triangle proportionality, and Pythagorean relationships.
Define right-triangle ratios and apply sine/cosine complementarity in models.
activities: Design an indirect-height measurement and justify the similar triangles.
Compare several similar right triangles to explain why a trigonometric ratio depends on the angle.
evidence: Explain a similarity proof without assuming the side ratios it must establish.
Choose a ratio from named opposite/adjacent sides and assess measurement limitations.
units.bridge: Triangle relationships explain many circle properties.

units.title: Circles and coordinate geometry
units.focus: Link synthetic relationships with equations and distance.
learning: Prove circle similarity and use chord, tangent, angle, incircle/circumcircle, and cyclic-quadrilateral relationships.
Derive circle/parabola equations and use coordinates for proofs, directed ratios, perimeter, and area.
activities: Construct a triangle center and investigate the distances that characterize it.
Derive a parabola from equal focus/directrix distances and use algebra to test a geometric conjecture.
evidence: Derive an arc-length/sector-area relationship and explain radian measure.
Complete a coordinate proof with valid slope/distance reasoning, handling vertical lines explicitly.
units.bridge: Plane figures become cross-sections and bases of solids.

units.title: Solids, density, and design
units.focus: Use geometric models with realistic constraints.
learning: Give informal arguments for circumference/area/volume formulas and identify cross-sections/solids of revolution.
Apply solid volumes, geometric approximations, density, and design tradeoffs.
activities: Compare two container designs meeting the same volume requirement and document simplifying assumptions.
Sketch solids generated by rotating plane regions and predict several cross-sections.
evidence: Explain a formula using decomposition or a limiting argument at an informal level.
Keep area/volume density units consistent and test whether a proposed design meets every constraint.
units.bridge: Design uncertainty can be analyzed through explicit chance models.

units.title: Conditional probability and decisions
units.focus: Use sets and tables to clarify what is being conditioned on.
learning: Represent events, calculate conditional probabilities, and distinguish independence from disjointness.
Use two-way tables and the addition rule to evaluate probability claims.
activities: Construct a two-way table for an invented classification process and compare P(A given B) with P(B given A).
Represent overlapping events with a sample-space diagram and test an independence claim.
evidence: State the conditional denominator and explain its meaning.
Justify independence with probabilities and account for overlap when finding a union.
units.bridge: Algebra 2 connects chance models to statistical inference and wider function families.

courses.title: Algebra 2 — suggested high-school pathway
courses.scopeNote: Suggested high-school placement, not a Common Core grade mandate. The standards specify conceptual categories across grades 9–12. (+) content is optional advanced preparation; revisit core standards as indicated.
prerequisites: Build linear/quadratic/exponential models and interpret regression.
Use Geometry proofs, radians, right-triangle ratios, and conditional probability.
outcomes: Analyze polynomial, radical, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions.
Use complex numbers to complete quadratic solving and justify equivalent forms/domain restrictions.
Use simulation, normal models, and study design to evaluate statistical conclusions.
courses.nextStep: Continue to Grade 12: This course completes the proposed placement of non-(+) high-school content; optional Grade 12 work extends functions, vectors, matrices, and probability.
courses.yearBridge: Extend polynomials into complex solutions, track domains in radical/rational work, study exponential/logarithmic and periodic functions, then combine statistical inference with a defended modeling investigation.
courses.crossSubject: Synthesize an equation, graph, and technical explanation; evaluate a study report by separating observed results, design choices, and justified inference.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Polynomials, roots, and complex numbers
units.focus: Extend algebraic structure beyond real quadratic roots.
learning: Operate on polynomials and use identities, factors, zeros, and the Remainder Theorem.
Define complex numbers, perform basic operations, and solve quadratics with nonreal roots.
Recognize even and odd functions from both graph symmetry and algebraic expressions, including functions that are neither.
activities: Construct polynomials with prescribed real zeros and compare algebraic factors with graph behavior.
Use completing the square to encounter a nonreal quadratic solution and check it by complex substitution.
Compare a quadratic, a cubic, and a translated version of each; substitute the opposite input and connect the resulting identities or failures to graph symmetry.
evidence: Explain a remainder as evaluation at the divisor zero.
Distinguish a real graph intercept from a nonreal algebraic root and verify a complex product.
Use f(−x) = f(x) or f(−x) = −f(x) on a symmetric domain to justify even or odd classification, and give a counterexample when neither identity holds.
units.bridge: Polynomial division and root structure support rational and radical equations.

units.title: Radicals, rational expressions, and inverses
units.focus: Track domains while transforming expressions and equations.
learning: Explain rational exponents and rewrite radical expressions; divide polynomials to rewrite rational expressions.
Solve simple rational/radical equations, identify extraneous roots, and find simple algebraic inverses.
Graph square-root and cube-root functions and their shifts, reflections, and scalings; explain their domains, intercepts, and endpoint or symmetry features.
activities: Compare an equation with its squared version and locate any newly admitted solutions.
Model a reversible quantity conversion, solve for its inverse, and connect its domain/range to the original.
Build tables and hand sketches for a square-root and a cube-root rule, transform each, and use a graphing tool to test the predicted changes.
evidence: State denominator and radical restrictions before solving and test all candidates.
Explain an inverse algebraically; full rational graph analysis and inverse-composition extensions are reserved for the optional pathway.
Produce labeled square-root and cube-root graphs with correct domains and features, and distinguish a square-root endpoint from a cube-root graph that continues in both directions.
units.bridge: Inverse thinking introduces logarithms as answers to exponential questions.

units.title: Exponential and logarithmic models
units.focus: Analyze multiplicative change over repeated intervals.
learning: Build/compare exponential models and express their solutions using logarithms, evaluated with technology as appropriate.
Derive finite geometric sums and connect recursive/explicit sequences with function transformations.
Build models by adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing standard function types, while interpreting the resulting quantities and domain restrictions.
activities: Compare an invented accumulating-payment plan with a single exponential deposit model.
Derive a finite geometric sum by aligning a series with a scaled copy, then interpret the result.
Model an invented decaying quantity above a fixed baseline by adding a constant and an exponential function; separately combine revenue and cost functions to model profit and average cost.
evidence: Explain the base, rate, and time unit in a model and justify a logarithmic solution.
Graph exponential/logarithmic functions with relevant intercepts and end behavior; distinguish discrete sequences from continuous models.
Write a combined function, explain each arithmetic operation in context, and identify any input excluded by a denominator; distinguish arithmetic combination from composition.
units.bridge: Periodic change requires a different function family.

units.title: Unit-circle and periodic models
units.focus: Extend triangle trigonometry to all real angle inputs.
learning: Interpret radians and define sine/cosine around the unit circle.
Model periodic quantities with amplitude, period, and midline; prove/use the Pythagorean identity.
activities: Generate a height model for a point moving on a circle and compare graph features with the motion.
Use unit-circle coordinates to justify the Pythagorean identity and determine a missing value with quadrant information.
evidence: Connect radian input to arc length and identify signs by quadrant.
Fit a periodic model to invented data and explain each parameter and the valid domain.
units.bridge: Models must also account for noisy data and statistical uncertainty.

units.title: Inference, simulation, and normal models
units.focus: Connect study design to the conclusions data can support.
learning: Use mean/standard deviation and a suitable normal model to estimate percentages.
Distinguish sampling from treatment randomization and use simulation for model checks, margins of error, and treatment comparisons.
activities: Simulate repeated samples from a known population and examine the spread of estimates.
Compare an observational report with a randomized experiment, then simulate a treatment difference under a chance-only model.
evidence: Explain when a normal model is inappropriate and use technology/tables accurately when it is appropriate.
State what population/generalization or causal claim a study design supports and describe simulation-based uncertainty.
units.bridge: Function models and statistical checks can be combined in a defensible investigation.

units.title: Comparing and defending models
units.focus: Integrate function families, constraints, and evidence.
learning: Compare linear, quadratic, polynomial, exponential, and periodic models using context and graphical evidence.
Communicate assumptions, precision, and statistical limits in a revised mathematical argument.
Explain why intersection input values solve f(x) = g(x), including linear, polynomial, rational, absolute-value, exponential, and logarithmic examples.
activities: Investigate a provided original dataset by fitting competing models and checking residuals and plausible domains.
Present a draft report, receive a peer challenge to an assumption, and revise the model or conclusion.
Compare an absolute-value tolerance rule with a linear cost rule, then use tables, graphing technology, or successive approximation to locate intersections across the other function families.
evidence: Justify a selected family with more than visual fit and verify a model-based equation solution.
Identify an extrapolation or causal claim the evidence cannot support and correct it.
Distinguish an intersection point from the input solving f(x) = g(x), verify approximate solutions in both functions, and respect domain restrictions for rational and logarithmic cases.
units.bridge: Students can now consolidate core mathematics or select optional advanced work suited to their goals.

courses.title: Advanced functions and modeling — optional pathway
courses.scopeNote: Optional advanced 36-week pathway after the core high-school sequence. It samples and connects every (+) numbered standard and the (+) subparts of F-IF.7d, F-BF.1c, and F-BF.4b–d; those subparts remain optional even though their parent registry entries also contain core content. The ambitious breadth needs local pacing and readiness decisions. It is not a mandated Grade 12 course and includes no compulsory calculus.
prerequisites: Complete core Algebra 2 and Geometry expectations or demonstrate equivalent readiness.
Use trigonometric functions, complex arithmetic, logarithmic models, and probability.
outcomes: Extend function analysis through composition, inverse restrictions, and rational graphs.
Apply advanced trigonometry, complex-plane geometry, vectors, and matrices.
Compare probabilistic decisions and develop a sustained model with justified limitations.
courses.nextStep: Choose further mathematics matched to goals: statistics, discrete mathematics, precalculus consolidation, or calculus after readiness review.
courses.yearBridge: Develop composition and inverse structure, deepen trigonometry, connect complex numbers and conics, use vectors and matrices, evaluate probability-based decisions, and synthesize selected methods in an investigation.
courses.crossSubject: Read a technical model critically, document assumptions, and write a sustained argument that distinguishes derivation, empirical evidence, and value judgments.
routines: Begin with a short retrieval task from an earlier unit and explain the method.
Compare two representations or solutions; revise an argument after a partner questions it.
Estimate before computing, choose tools deliberately, and finish with a unit or reasonableness check.

units.title: Composition, inverses, and rational functions
units.focus: Optional (+) extensions develop precise function structure.
learning: Compose functions and verify inverses by composition, tables, graphs, and suitable domain restrictions.
Analyze rational zeros/asymptotes/end behavior, perform rational-expression arithmetic, and use the Binomial Theorem.
Use the inverse relationship between exponential and logarithmic functions to solve problems and explain the relevant base and domain restrictions.
activities: Model a chain of conversions as a composition and show why reversing the order changes its meaning.
Compare a rational expression before and after cancellation, preserving any missing domain point; derive a binomial expansion by structure.
Reverse an exponential calibration rule with a logarithm, then check the two compositions on valid inputs and interpret the result in the original units.
evidence: State the domain of a composition and verify an inverse on that domain.
Distinguish a removable discontinuity from an asymptote and justify an expansion or rational simplification.
Translate consistently between logarithmic and exponential statements and verify a resulting solution while requiring a positive logarithm argument and a valid base.
units.bridge: Function restrictions make inverse trigonometric reasoning precise.

units.title: Advanced trigonometry
units.focus: Optional (+) extensions link identities, inverses, and nonright triangles.
learning: Derive special-angle values and unit-circle symmetry; prove/use addition/subtraction formulas.
Restrict trigonometric domains for inverses and solve periodic models and nonright triangles using sine/cosine laws.
activities: Derive a compound-angle value two ways and compare exact results.
